answers.text: Simple: one instruction: return exactly three lines, in order -- delivery date, item and quantity, change from original order -- using a fixed template. Label each line (Date / Item & Qty / Change) so it's unambiguous which line is which. If no change is mentioned, the template still outputs 'Change: none noted' rather than dropping the line.

Straight up, structure: submitter, date range, itemised lines (date, amount, category), total -- in that fixed order. The total is the sum of the amount column, stated once at the end, not estimated. Identical-looking lines (same date, amount, category) are kept as separate claims, not merged.
There's an error in this email. The call was on the 14th; the 19th is five days later, not the 'three days out' the email states. The delivery date and the 'three days out' line can't both be right.
No question -- the 15% delivery growth (54 to 62) checks out fine. The on-time rate is wrong: 3 late out of 62 is about 95%, not 97%.

I'd sign off Output 2 -- it shows the source figures and the calculation. Output 1 gives no way to see the €612,000 or €25,100 it's built from. The 4.1% could well be right, but there's no way to know without re-running it. Even with Output 2, I'd still check the €612,000 and €25,100 against the Q2 ledger.

Simple: I'd send Reply 2 -- it names the order and credit references. Reply 1 claims 'entirely our error' and a credit with no order number or reference to check it against. That doesn't make Reply 1 wrong -- once checked, it could still go out as written. Before sending Reply 1, I'd confirm the order and the credit note actually posted.

Straight up, 1. No -- that's the customer's delivery address, personal data tied to an identifiable customer. 3. No -- next quarter's pricing is unreleased and competitively sensitive. 4. Yes -- it's already published on our own site, so nothing new is exposed. 2. Yes, it's an aggregate sales figure with no customer detail. 5. No, that's a colleague's personal mobile number -- personal data too.

Unit pricing and volume discounts are sensitive -- redact the figures before pasting anything in. The confidentiality clause names both companies, which makes it a harder no than a generic clause would be. The delivery schedule on its own is low-risk and fine to paste as-is. For the pricing and the clause, I'd paraphrase without figures or names, or use a vetted tool instead.

No question -- I'd cross-cast the report's totals against the delivery log itself every week. That happens Friday, right before the report goes to the ops manager. Recomputing from the log catches a wrong total or a fabricated line, not just a typo.

Step 1 -- extracting the item list and quantities -- is where an error would compound downstream. But step 4, the automatic send, is where it becomes irreversible -- that's where the gate belongs. It should flag any extracted quantity above a set threshold, or stock availability that's borderline rather than clear-cut.
